query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled volume fraction of ductile-transformable B2 precipitates into the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy will enhance mechanical integrity, reducing crack formation, while retaining its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The as-synthesized (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but suffers from poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack.
generation.intervention: Apply a targeted heat-treatment and/or micro-alloying process designed to precipitate a controlled fraction (e.g., ~10-20% by volume) of ductile-transformable multicomponent B2 intermetallic phases into the alloy.
generation.conditions: Under the same applied magnetic and pressure fields and within the temperature range optimal for the caloric effect. The loading regime includes cyclic mechanical stresses typical of practical applications where both caloric performance and structural integrity are required.
generation.structural_mediator: Ductile-transformable B2 precipitates that form a coherent dispersion within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: The B2 precipitates are expected to undergo reversible martensitic transformation, which absorbs and dissipates strain energy during cyclic loading. This mechanism delays crack nucleation and propagation while not interfering significantly with the caloric phase transformation in the matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will demonstrate improved compressive strength and fatigue resistance (e.g., an improvement of 25–50% over the untreated alloy) with caloric response maintained within 5–10% of that of the unchanged alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, exhibiting high caloric performance but poor mechanical integrity, particularly under cyclic loading conditions.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if the precipitate volume fraction, morphology, and distribution are tightly controlled. Excess precipitate content or improper processing conditions may result in diminished caloric response or even new sources of mechanical degradation. The operating conditions (temperature, applied-field, pressure) must remain within ranges that preserve the stability of both the caloric phase and the precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters for inducing the desired B2 precipitate structure and its precise interaction with the alloy’s caloric phase are not fully determined. There is uncertainty regarding the tolerance of the caloric mechanism to the additional phase interfaces introduced by the precipitates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one group undergoing the controlled heat-treatment/micro-alloying process to form B2 precipitates, and a control group without such treatment. Subject both groups to identical applied-field, pressure and temperature cycling as well as cyclic mechanical loading.
measurements: Fatigue life (through cyclic load testing until crack initiation)
Caloric effect magnitude (adiabatic temperature change or entropy change under field/pressure cycling)
Microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM to verify precipitate structure and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit an improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., a >25% increase in compressive strength or prolonged fatigue life) while retaining a caloric response within 10% of the control sample’s performance, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
AbstractCatastrophic accidents caused by fatigue failures often occur in engineering structures. Thus, a fundamental understanding of cyclic-deformation and fatigue-failure mechanisms is critical for the development of fatigue-resistant structural materials. Here we report a high-entropy alloy with enhanced fatigue life by ductile-transformable multicomponent B2 precipitates. Its cyclic-deformation mechanisms are revealed by real-time in-situ neutron diffraction, transmission-electron microscopy, crystal-plasticity modeling, and Monte-Carlo simulations. Multiple cyclic-deformation mechanisms, including dislocation slips, precipitation strengthening, deformation twinning, and reversible martensitic phase transformation, are observed in the studied high-entropy alloy. Its improved fatigue performance at low strain amplitudes, i.e., the high fatigue-crack-initiation resistance, is attributed to the high elasticity, plastic deformability, and martensitic transformation of the B2-strengthening phase. This study shows that fatigue-resistant alloys can be developed by incorporating strengthening ductile-transformable multicomponent intermetallic phases.Subject terms: Mechanica
